title: Justice Department Housing Discrimination Case Against Trump Management
description_short: DOJ sued Donald and Fred Trump’s company in 1973 over alleged rental discrimination; a 1975 consent decree imposed fair-housing requirements.
description_medium: The Justice Department sued Donald Trump, Fred Trump and Trump Management in 1973, alleging Fair Housing Act violations in rental housing. The complaint said Black applicants were denied vacancy information or steered elsewhere. A 1975 consent decree barred discriminatory rental practices and required fair-housing advertising, training and weekly vacancy lists for the New York Urban League. The decree said it was not an admission of a violation.
description_long: In October 1973, the Justice Department sued Donald Trump, his father Fred Trump and Trump Management in federal court in Brooklyn, alleging Fair Housing Act violations at 39 buildings with more than 14,000 apartments. The complaint described paired tests in which white testers were told about vacancies while Black testers were not or were directed to other properties. It also alleged that employees used codes beside applicants’ names to indicate race. Trump and his company counterclaimed for defamation, but the court dismissed that claim and allowed the government’s case to proceed. The parties settled through a consent decree signed June 10, 1975. It barred discrimination in rental terms and practices, required fair-housing statements in advertisements and required Donald and Fred Trump to familiarize themselves with the Act. Trump Management also had to provide weekly vacancy lists to the New York Urban League for two years. The decree expressly said the settlement was not an admission of a Fair Housing Act violation.

facts: The Justice Department filed the 1973 Fair Housing Act case against Donald Trump, Fred Trump and Trump Management.
The case file describes the complaint’s allegations, dismissal of the defendants’ counterclaim, and June 10, 1975 consent decree.
The decree barred specified discriminatory practices, imposed advertising/training and vacancy-list requirements, and disclaimed an admission of liability.

rationale: Pass after the single supplied case-file lead was checked and confirmed the alleged practices, consent decree, and no-admission clause. The corrected short copy removes the truncated ending; the Clearinghouse URL is added as the supporting source, while the timed-out Washington Post link is not relied on.

description_short: Newsweek reported Trump Hotels paid $68,551.88 for a 1998 Cuba business trip; it described a possible embargo violation, not a government fine.
